skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The Preface is a famous voice-signature meta-statement; nothing in it is required by the synopsis, and any 'kernel' (the manikin metaphor) would mood-break the opening Quincy chapter.

The second half of the Berlin chapter (German high-school routine and the awakening to Beethoven) elaborates material the synopsis already fixes in one phrase; only the Beethoven epiphany and 'hard limits of memory' lesson must be preserved.
skippable_chapters.kernel: What Berlin's Gymnasium and university failed to teach, an accidental afternoon in a beer-hall did: amid stale tobacco and Hausfrauen knitting, Beethoven's symphonic line stole into Adams's unconscious and opened a sense he had not known he possessed, even as the German drill on memory taught him its hard limits.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The continuation of Chapter VIII (London social mortifications, Bull Run reaction, Trent Affair details, Mount Felix) supplies texture the synopsis abstracts as 'London society entertains, resents, and educates him by indifference.' The Trent beat itself is preserved in the kernel.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Then came the Trent Affair: the seizure of Mason and Slidell brought the Legation to the brink of war, and the Minister, summoned from Yorkshire, met the crisis without losing his nerve. The shock passed; the secretaries learned that patience, silence, and the closing of newspaper indiscretions were the only diplomacy left to them.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: This is the second half of the Palmerston/Russell/Gladstone analysis (Gladstone's confession, Granville letters, Morley footnotes) — an essayistic post-mortem repeating the chapter's already-stated lesson that the Minister could not trust British professions.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Forty years later, Gladstone's own confession revealed that the Cabinet's drift toward intervention had been even nearer success than Adams had supposed; the lesson stood, that in politics no professed friend in power could be trusted, and that the diplomatic victory of 1862 had been won against men who scarcely knew their own minds.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: Continuation of the eccentricity essay (Bright at Lowell's dinner, Henry Reeve, the doctrinaire class) — pure character-typology with no plot consequence.

Second half of the Darwinism chapter (Pteraspis cousinship, Bank Restriction articles, North American Review placement) is an extended scientific-financial digression; only the lesson that 'Evolution that did not evolve' shaped Adams's later doubt needs to survive.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Out of his Wenlock musings on Pteraspis Adams carried forward only the suspicion that evolution offered no proof of progress, and that the unity science promised was, like religion, a working hypothesis a historian should accept on faith or not at all.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: Second half of the Harvard professorship chapter (faculty-room sterility, editorship of the NAR, first Western trip with Emmons and meeting King) repeats the synopsis's compressed verdict on teaching; only the meeting with King is load-bearing and can be relocated.
skippable_chapters.kernel: When the year's teaching was done, Adams escaped westward, and on the slope of Long's Peak fell, by happy accident, into the arms of Clarence King — geologist, wit, and ideal American — whose friendship, begun in a one-cabin Estes Park, would last as long as either lived.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The brief coda to Chapter XXII (the silver-vote night, capitulation to the gold standard) is a postscript whose substance the synopsis covers under 'Panic of 1893 strips him of illusions.'
skippable_chapters.kernel: The vote came; the gold standard won; and Adams, with his eighteenth-century prejudices, accepted that the capitalistic system had absorbed his class along with the rest, leaving only the question how long and how far its acceleration would run.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: Second half of the Dynamo and Virgin chapter (St. Gaudens at Amiens, Renaissance digression, scholastic-science survey) elaborates material the synopsis distills as 'against [the dynamo] he sets the Virgin of Chartres'; the central Virgin/Dynamo opposition is already stated in Ch 036.
skippable_chapters.kernel: From the Virgin he passed to her artist: St. Gaudens at Amiens revealed how the modern American could feel the cathedral's dignity but no longer the force that built it, and Adams understood that the energy he sought to measure had become, for his countrymen, only a question of taste.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The Twilight chapter's geological survey (ganoid fish revisited, Lord Kelvin, Suess, larger synthesis) is essayistic recapitulation whose conclusions are restated and extended in the Dynamic Theory chapters that close the book.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Hay's diplomatic triumph in China lifted Adams's spirits, but King's collapse and Hay's failing health darkened the season; meanwhile the magnet on Adams's desk, and the geologists' confessions of ignorance, warned him that the unity he had sought all his life was dissolving into a multiplicity science could no longer pretend to govern.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: An untitled coda to Ch 040 elaborating Hay's coal-power/gun-power diplomacy; the synopsis's references to the Open Door and the Atlantic system are already carried by Chs 040 and 043.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Hay's last triumphs—drawing England, France, and even Germany toward an Atlantic combine while Russia alone remained intractable—seemed to Adams the highest reach a scholar of statesmanship could witness, even as he confessed that such mastery only deepened his sense of his own ignorance.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: A self-contained essay on Pearson, Poincaré, Mach, and Haeckel whose thesis is already carried by the synopsis's line that Adams 'reads Karl Pearson and Poincaré' and accepts that science has sailed beyond unity.
skippable_chapters.kernel: Reading Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science and Poincaré's La Science et l'Hypothèse, Adams heard beneath their equations the whisper that order was a convenience and chaos the only honest assertion science could make of the supersensual; even Euclidian geometry, Poincaré allowed, was not true but merely convenient. Science had abandoned unity, and the child of 1900 would be born into a multiverse rather than a universe.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The Dynamic Theory of History essay is precisely the formula the synopsis names; its argument can be distilled into the surviving frame.
skippable_chapters.kernel: From these soundings Adams shaped a Dynamic Theory of History: man as a feeble atom captured by the attractive forces of nature, his progress measurable as the assimilation of new energies—from fetish and Cross to compass and gunpowder—each accelerating his orbit toward an unknown perihelion.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: The Law of Acceleration chapter restates in essay form what the synopsis already names as a Law of Acceleration measurable in coal and horsepower.
skippable_chapters.kernel: To this dynamic theory Adams added a Law of Acceleration: coal-output doubling every decade, force compounding upon force, the human meteor drawn ever faster toward a perihelion at which the mind itself would have to leap into a new equilibrium or be dissipated.
